newsitem.title: USA: Divided House wants to move beyond Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Divided House wants to move beyond Gingrich.

text.p: Frustrated Republicans hoped Tuesday's historic House vote to punish Speaker Newt Gingrich would take the political spotlight off his ethics problems, letting them move forward with a broad legislative agenda.

But Republicans were bitter and divided as the years-long investigation of Gingrich finally came to an end -- some complaining the reprimand and $300,000 penalty approved by the House were far too harsh and set a troubling precedent.
They worried the first-ever vote to punish a House speaker had diminished Gingrich's power and with it the influence of House Republicans in coming battles with the White House.

While saying they longed to begin work on initiatives like a balanced budget, Republicans wondered if they could cut deals with Democrats after the partisan battle. They also needed to mend rifts within their own party, leaving after the vote for a three-day retreat in Warrenton, Virginia, with Gingrich.
"Everybody says this gives us a great opportunity to move forward. I don't know. What is the next set of ethics charges to get filed?" said House Budget Committee chair John Kasich.
"Maybe the next step beyond the $300,000 ... is that we put people in stockades out on the front steps of the Capitol and throw vegetables at them," the Ohio Republican said.

Democrats also seemed eager to turn down the volume, with Gingrich's main critic, Michigan Representative David Bonior, saying he would take a lower profile and let Republicans "decide whether this is the kind of person they want to be their leader."
The House voted 395-28 to punish Gingrich. The $300,000 penalty was the largest ever levied in an ethics case.

Gingrich agreed to the punishment in what amounted to a plea bargain with the ethics panel. The Georgia Republican, narrowly re-elected as speaker earlier this month, has admitted to providing false information to the panel about a controversial college course and violating House rules.

Ohio Representative John Boehner, echoing the sentiments of many Republicans, said the party wanted to quickly put the ethics problems aside and focus on issues. He admitted it could take some time for Republicans to regain their political footing.

"Is this unsettling to members? Yes. Are some members more concerned than others? Yes," Boehner said. As the White House and Republicans began to work together, he said "every day that goes by (Gingrich) strengthens himself."
Moderate Maryland Republican Representative Connie Morella, who did not vote for Gingrich when he narrowly won re-election as speaker earlier this month, was more blunt.
"Newt has a lot to offer in terms of intelligence and in terms of vision. Now he's going to have to re-establish credibility," Morella said.

Nine Republicans did not back Gingrich for speaker in a vote held before the ethics report and $300,000 penalty was released. Republican leaders had characterised the expected punishment as minor before the report was released.
New York Representative Michael Forbes, another Republican who broke with Gingrich, said the ethics travails had caused rifts.
"Some people in the conference think some of us are disloyal. Others have very great troubles with this, but walked the plank. Those feelings don't die easily," he said.
